summary:
Stomatal density is the number of stomata per square millimetre of leaf surface — the structural limit on how fast a leaf can take up carbon dioxide. It returns area sampled, stomatal density, stomatal density and pore index, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator converts a count in a microscope field into density per mm² and per cm². The arithmetic keeps full precision internally and only rounds what it displays, so the number you copy out is the number the formula produced. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Stomatal Density
sections.html:
Density = stomata ÷ (fields × π × (diameter/2)²)

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
stomatastomata counted across all fieldsstomata
fieldsnumber of microscope fieldsfields
diameterfield-of-view diameter at that magnificationmm

sections.title: How do I use the Stomatal Density?
sections.html:
Fill the boxes you have numbers for; the calculator decides what it can derive from them.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: stomata counted of 46 stomata, fields counted of 5, field of view diameter of 2.2 mm, stomatal pore index (optional) of 0.0021 mm².

Substituting them into the formula gives area sampled of 19.01 mm², stomatal density of 2.42 per mm², stomatal density of 242.02 per cm², pore index of 0.0051.

Because the example uses the defaults, you can reproduce it by loading the page and reading the results panel before touching anything.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
Interpretation is a convention, not part of the arithmetic. The usual bands are:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
below 100 per mm²Lowthick-leaved, shade or water-limited species
100 – 300Typicalmost mesophytic crop and wild species
above 400Highsun-adapted grasses and fast-growing herbs

  • Count on the abaxial (lower) surface of a dicot leaf and either surface of a grass; the two surfaces differ by a factor of two or more.

  • Stomatal density falls with rising atmospheric CO₂ and rises with growth temperature and light — which is why fossil leaves are used as palaeoclimate proxies.

  • Density is not conductance: guard-cell aperture and behaviour matter as much as count.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
Before blaming the formula, check these — they explain nearly every mismatch:

  • Forgetting to convert the field diameter from micrometres.
  • Counting only the top surface of a leaf whose stomata are mostly underneath.
  • Using a nail-varnish peel without noting which surface it came from.

faq.q: How do I calculate stomatal density?
faq.a: Divide the number of stomata by the area of the field(s) they were counted in.
Density on the upper surface divided by density on the lower, about 0 for most trees and about 1 for grasses.

faq.q: What does the Stomatal Density actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns area sampled, stomatal density, stomatal density and pore index. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
